source.title: A Low-Rank Subspace Analysis of LLM Interventions
source.authors: Angira Sharma; C. D. de Witt; P. Torr; A. Calinescu; Jia-Lin Yu

page_placements.theme: Category and topic structure: shared refusal component, category-specific harm parts, topic-specific (political) refusal

record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares rank-1 with higher-rank behavior representations and intervenes by projecting out behavior subspaces. It reports that rank-1 interventions are weaker, that rank-2 interventions affect multiple refusal categories, and that effects can be asymmetric or collateral. This refines the single-direction account rather than reproducing its exact method.
record.gate_note: The study uses centered contrastive activation differences, PCA-derived subspaces, and projection interventions at selected layers and the last token. It does not test adding a refusal direction, ablation at every layer and position, actual compliance/refusal rates, or general capabilities. Pairwise geometry and cross-category matrices are extensively reported; the rows below prioritize rank ablations, category self-effects, and aggregate collateral effects. Descriptive values used only for analysis or selection are not included as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: Only the rank-1 versus rank-2/3 ablation bears on V4, and weakly: it is one model, one layer, and uses category subspaces from centered PCA. The paper argues single-direction models of behaviour are insufficient. It never builds or ablates the difference-in-means refusal direction, because centering removes the mean offset. So V1 is not tested. The contrasts are instructed-REFUSE versus instructed-COMPLY system prompts, not harmful versus harmless requests.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that behaviours are better modelled as interacting low-rank subspaces. Overlap marks where cross-behaviour effects can occur, and alignment with a decision subspace modulates their size and direction. Effects are asymmetric and model-dependent, which limits treating behaviours as isolated directions.
record.recipe_differences: The study extracts centered PCA subspaces from matched contrastive activation differences, removes decision-aligned components for geometric analysis, and projects out raw category subspaces at selected layers and the last token. It uses rank 2 by default rather than one mean-difference direction, and does not test adding a direction or ablation at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with category, model, layer, and subspace rank. The study reports rank-1 weaker effects and rank-3 higher collateral effects; intervention effects are localized by layer and vary across model families. It also reports sensitivity of overlap-effect correlations to the decision-subspace rank kdec.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting out one refusal category's subspace shifts refusal margins of other categories, often as much as its own. In Gemma, removing Copyright or NSFW subspaces increases refusal; effects are asymmetric and model-dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Category-specific refusal subspaces are not separable: ablating one category's subspace changes refusal on other categories, sometimes raising refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned rank-2 category subspaces produce margin effects 147x-319x larger than random rank-2 subspaces.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-related learned subspaces, unlike random ones, causally shift refusal margins.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (as stated)
record.problems: Interventions are projection-based and evaluated using log-probability decision margins rather than refusal/compliance rates. The study does not test general capabilities, direction addition, or ablation at every layer and position. Main synthetic refusal data are constructed with generated prompts and fixed response templates; intervention results are layer- and category-dependent. Many intervention-effect entries have no reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional cross-category matrices for refusal, jailbreak, and sycophancy, as well as layer-wise effects and geometry results. These were not individually extracted because they concern broader cross-category structure rather than the rank-1-versus-low-rank result, and the table also reports extensive aggregate collateral effects. No results were omitted from the rank-ablation table or the self-intervention table used above.

untested.parts: All of V1. No difference-in-means direction: contrasts are centered before PCA, removing the mean offset. No addition, no all-layer/all-position ablation, no refusal rates, no capability check.
Jailbreak prompts are used only as category data. No attack-mechanism or robustness test.
Affine and cone formulations. No comparison against the original single refusal direction. Rank ablation only in Gemma-2-9B at layer -8, plus one category pair in Tables 24-25.

missing.what: Rank-1 vs private vs full-subspace self and collateral effects across alpha for Deceptive/Malicious→NSFW. Rank-1 self is 0.14 (Gemma) and 0.36 (Llama) at alpha=1, vs 3.26 and 2.20 for the full rank-2 subspace.
Decision subspace is low-rank: top two decision-aligned PCs explain most margin-correlated variance (about 60-80% in several models). Mistral is more diffuse.
missing.locator: Section 3.3; Appendix C Fig. 13; Appendix L.5.2 Fig. 24

record.verdict_notes: Key caveats for V1/V4. (1) Contrasts are instructed-REFUSE vs instructed-COMPLY system prompts on the same request, not harmful vs harmless instructions. (2) Centering before PCA removes the mean-difference vector, so the study's rank-1 direction is not Arditi's refusal direction. Its claim that rank-1 is insufficient therefore does not bear on V1. (3) The outcome is a REFUSE/COMPLY label log-prob margin, not generated refusal rates. (4) Large near-uniform collateral effects, e.g. Mistral Against Policy/NSFW at about -15 on every category, are as consistent with a shared refusal component as with multi-directionality. The record's V1 limits_scope label and the random-null 'supports V4' label were dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests rank-1 versus rank-2 projection effects on refusal margins, but not the original mean-difference direction at every layer and position, adding the direction, actual compliance rates, or preservation of general capabilities.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
The jailbreak dataset is used to analyze refusal-category subspaces; the study does not test whether attacks suppress this direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Tests low-rank subspaces and rank-1 versus rank-2/rank-3 interventions, not affine or cone formulations specifically.
No separate harmfulness judgment versus refusal-decision experiment.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or matched model-variant transfer test.
No comparison of refusal training procedures or training stages.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-9B-IT, synthetic refusal, layer -8, category subspaces from centered PCA of instructed refuse/comply contrasts
relationships.reason: Projecting out rank-2 category subspaces moves the refusal margin about twice as much as rank-1 (4.3 vs 2.1), with no gain at rank-3 (4.2). Weak: removing more dimensions may mechanically give larger effects, and the single refusal direction was never compared (R1, R3, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Rank-two removal shifted the refusal margin by 4.3 versus 2.1 for rank one and 4.2 for rank three, although dimensionality effects and comparison with the standard refusal direction remained unresolved.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Gemma-2-9B-IT, synthetic refusal, layer -8, category subspaces from centered PCA of instructed refuse/comply contrasts
source_check.reason: Table 2 confirms mean self |ΔM| of 2.1 (r=1), 4.3 (r=2) and 4.2 (r=3). The study reports rank-1 is insufficient (App. D, Sec. 5). Weak support. The subspaces are nested and the rank-1 comparator is the top centered PC, not the diff-in-means direction. Collateral also rises (1.2 to 3.8), so the gain is not refusal-specific. One model, one layer.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Gemma-2-9B-IT, synthetic refusal, layer -8, category subspaces from centered PCA of instructed refuse/comply contrasts
labels.reason: Table 2 confirms mean self |ΔM| of 2.1 (r=1), 4.3 (r=2) and 4.2 (r=3). The study reports rank-1 is insufficient (App. D, Sec. 5). Weak support. The subspaces are nested and the rank-1 comparator is the top centered PC, not the diff-in-means direction. Collateral also rises (1.2 to 3.8), so the gain is not refusal-specific. One model, one layer.

relation.reason: Its own rank ablation measures how the refusal margin changes as more contrast dimensions are projected out, which bears on V4. It never builds or ablates the difference-in-means direction, so the test is weak and indirect.

tranche.reason: Contribution 2 argues for models beyond single-direction behaviour representations. The paper cites Arditi's dominant direction and says isolated-direction models are limited. Its own results bearing on the claim (rank-1 vs rank-2/3 ablation, Table 2) are an argument that the single-direction picture needs restating.

source_check.notes: All 25 rows match the text. Contrasts are same request under LEARN_REFUSE vs LEARN_COMPLY system prompts (App. A), not harmful vs harmless, and centering removes the mean contrast, so no Arditi-style direction is built. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is accurate. The paper also reports a decision subspace whose top-2 PCs carry most margin-correlated variance (App. E, Fig. 13/24); this is not in the rows and is variance-explained only, not causal.

statements.correction: Context, nothing wrong: 147x-319x is the self |ΔM| / random-null ratio averaged over the last 12 layers (Llama 319x, Gemma 198x, Mistral 147x). Per-layer ratios run 11x-1349x (Table 4). App. F prose says 24x-319x.
statements.problem: None found. Cross-category shifts are often comparable to self-effects (Fig. 2 caption). Max collateral matches or exceeds self in all three models (Table 1). In Gemma, Copyright- and NSFW-source projections give positive ΔM on every target (Table 35; App. L.1, L.6). 147x-319x matches Table 1/Table 5.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Rank-1 projection in Gemma-2-9B-IT on synthetic refusal prompts at layer -8
reader_labels.reason: The study reports weak rank-1 self-effects (2.1 mean |∆M|) and says rank-1 is insufficient for category-specific structure; this is not evidence that one direction removes refusal fully or preserves general capability (R1).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Rank ablation in Gemma-2-9B-IT on synthetic refusal prompts at layer -8
reader_labels.reason: Rank-2 has larger mean self-effects than rank-1, while the study characterizes rank-1 as insufficient; it treats behavior representations as distributed across multiple directions (R1-R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Rank-3 projection and rank-2 cross-category interventions in the reported models
reader_labels.reason: Rank-3 raises collateral effects, and rank-2 projection effects are not isolated: maximum collateral effects meet or exceed mean self-effects, with category- and model-specific margin changes (R5-R8, R10-R14, R16-R30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Random rank-2 projection controls versus learned subspaces across three models
reader_labels.reason: Random-subspace effects are much smaller than learned-subspace effects, supporting a role for structured, multi-dimensional representations rather than generic projection alone (R9, R12, R15).
